summary: Serves as the entry point to the documents about Congestion Exposure (ConEx). It explains the motivation for adding a ConEx marking at the IP layer so that information about congestion is visible to network nodes, and focuses on how this could be used. It is informational.

eli5.summary: On a busy road, drivers know about traffic, but the road operators may not. ConEx lets traffic show how crowded it is so everyone can see.

questions: why expose congestion at the ip layer
how does conex improve traffic management
subtitle: Exposing congestion information at the IP layer for better traffic management.

tldr.problem: Network operators cannot easily see which users or flows are causing congestion, making it difficult to manage traffic fairly. Congestion feedback only reaches the transport layer, not the network operators who need it.
tldr.mechanism: ConEx marks IP packets to expose whole-path congestion information. Senders read congestion feedback from the transport layer and re-inject it as IP-layer marks that any network node can read and act on.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can implement congestion-aware traffic management, protecting users from others' disproportionate contribution to congestion while rewarding applications that back off quickly when congestion occurs.

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Informational, entry point to ConEx suite

today: RFC 6789 is informational and serves as an entry point to the ConEx protocol family. It has not been obsoleted. The technology is experimental and has seen deployment trials, but has not become a standard Internet protocol.

sections.title: How Congestion Feedback Works Today
sections.content:
The Internet uses packet switching: many users share a network link. When too much traffic arrives at a link, congestion happens: packets get delayed or dropped, or marked with Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) signals.

Today, the receiver detects these congestion signals and sends congestion feedback back to the sender, which slows down. But network operators cannot see this feedback. They only see the total traffic rate, not how much congestion each user causes. This makes it hard to manage fairly: a user causing lots of congestion looks the same as a user sending a steady, well-behaved stream.
sections.eli5: When a road gets crowded, drivers feel the traffic and slow down. But the road managers can only count how many cars passed, not how many were stuck in traffic. So they cannot tell who caused the jam.

sections.title: Congestion Volume and Rest-of-Path Congestion
sections.content:
ConEx introduces two key ideas. Congestion-volume is the amount of data a user sent that got lost or marked during congestion, measured in bytes. If Alice sends 1 GB while 0.2% of packets are lost, she caused 2 MB of congestion-volume. This metric lets operators hold each user accountable for their contribution.

Rest-of-path congestion (or downstream congestion) is the congestion a flow will experience between a measurement point and its destination. By comparing the congestion marked at the IP layer (whole-path) with the ECN signals seen so far (upstream), operators can estimate rest-of-path congestion. This helps them understand where congestion is happening.
sections.eli5: Congestion-volume is like counting how many people got stuck in traffic because of one car. Rest-of-path congestion is guessing how bad the traffic will be for the rest of the trip.

sections.title: The Core Use Case: Congestion-Aware Traffic Management
sections.content:
The primary benefit of ConEx is enabling fair congestion-aware traffic management. A network operator places a congestion policer at the network edge to monitor each user's ConEx signals and enforce congestion-volume quotas. The policer works like a token bucket, but instead of counting data bytes, it counts the amount of congestion each user causes.

When the network is uncongested, all users can send freely. When congestion appears and a user exhausts their quota, the network can drop, delay, or deprioritize that user's traffic. Users whose applications back off when they detect congestion (like LEDBAT, a scavenger transport protocol) use less of their congestion quota, creating incentives for congestion-aware applications.
sections.eli5: Each driver gets a 'congestion budget': they can cause only so much traffic jam per month. Drivers who are careful and slow down during jams get rewarded. Drivers who rush through jams get slowed down until they behave.

sections.title: How ConEx Can Be Deployed Incrementally
sections.content:
ConEx is designed for gradual rollout. Even if only some senders support ConEx, a network on the path benefits: it can reward ConEx-enabled senders by treating them more leniently than non-ConEx senders. This bootstraps adoption, because senders have incentive to adopt ConEx to avoid being over-policed.

TCP implementations need modification to send ConEx marks (as described in companion RFCs). Most TCP receivers already support SACK (Selective Acknowledgment), which provides the feedback ConEx senders need. Networks simply place congestion policers at their ingress points, like they do with DiffServ.

Feasible initial scenarios exist for broadband access networks, mobile networks, and data centers. Some can work without ECN support; data centers benefit most from ECN.
sections.eli5: One company can start using ConEx for their network. Other companies can do the same when they want. It works even if not everyone has it yet.

sections.title: Comparison with Existing Traffic Management
sections.content:
Rate-based approaches limit users' peak or average bit rate, but risk over- or under-constraining the network. Volume-based approaches cap total data per month, regardless of whether the network is congested, and do not reward congestion-aware applications. Application-based approaches inspect traffic to identify applications and rate-limit certain ones, but conflict with encryption and raise privacy concerns.

ConEx offers advantages: it only acts during congestion, reacts proportionately to each user's contribution, provides transparent metrics both providers and customers can verify, and encourages development of scavenger transports. Unlike existing approaches, it can reduce both performance uncertainty and billing uncertainty for users.
sections.eli5: Old ways either limit everyone equally (unfair when some drive better than others) or count total cars without knowing how much they caused traffic. ConEx counts actual damage and is fair.
